# Conclusion {#sec-discussion-outlook}

## Summary
Returning to the three questions: demand is highly concentrated in space and time. Downtown (the Loop and Near North Side) accounts for roughly 40 % of pickups and O'Hare for a further 21 %, while the daily cycle runs from near zero overnight to a peak around 17:00 (@sec-data-analytics). Community areas are the unit best suited for fleet management, being complete, free of interpolation artefacts and small enough (roughly three square miles) to act on, whereas census tracts are too sparse and privacy-suppressed to trust. At this resolution demand is well predictable from calendar, weather and location alone. The feed-forward network reaches an R² of 0.90–0.93 and, at the recommended 4-hour/community-area resolution, cuts the error of a naive historical-average baseline by roughly 18 % (nMAE 0.25 against 0.31, @sec-demand-prediction). Its additional complexity is therefore justified, as unlike the SVR it trains on the full multi-million-row dataset and stays stable at finer resolutions where the SVR degrades. Lastly, home charging of an EV taxi can be optimized with reinforcement learning. A tabular Monte Carlo agent cuts charging cost by about 50 % against a naive full-charge baseline while keeping energy shortfalls to 0.14 % of episodes (@sec-rl), matching or exceeding a Deep Q-Network while being far easier and cheaper to train, particularly during hyperparameter search an advantage that holds only as long as the state and action spaces stay small enough for a tabular agent.

## Discussion & Limitations
For the fleet operator, these results translate into concrete operational guidance.
The network's community-area, 4-hour forecasts are precise enough to steer vehicle
pre-positioning: supply should be concentrated at airports and downtown, with active
rebalancing back from the airport given its pickup-heavy asymmetry, and buffered
ahead of the evening peak and around weekends and holidays, where the demand *level*
shifts but not its *geography*. On charging, the RL results show that optimizing at-home
charging using smart agents has a high benefit under an exponential cost structure, where
higher charging power costs more, since the operator directly controls timing and can shift
power to the cheapest, lowest-power slots. Private home or depot charging should therefore be the primary channel, since the saving depends on being able to control the power level. Public charging is a complement for long shifts and airport waiting time rather than a substitute.

Still, there are multiple limitations to consider. Most fundamentally, the dataset records
completed trips rather than demand, so rides that were wanted but never served leave no
trace and a fleet allocated on realised trips entrenches existing supply gaps instead of
closing them. Taxis are also only a partial proxy for ride-hailing, since street hailing
and airport stands concentrate trips at classic taxi hotspots in a way app-based ordering
does not. Both argue for validating the forecasts against the client's own booking data.
Beyond that, the demand models do not include the exact year and date to avoid overfitting, but this prevents the models from learning a multi-year trend such as rising trip volumes in growing areas. Capturing this would require adding the feature back deliberately or retraining the model regularly as new data arrives. The point-of-interest features are static snapshots that cannot reflect how the POI landscape changes over time, a limitation we accept because static POIs still help the model relate similar areas to one another. The census tract layer is constrained by Chicago's privacy suppression, which strips tract information from low-frequency trips and affects more than half of all records. Furthermore, tract boundaries may have shifted within the observation window, influencing the predictions. These conditions mean that many spatio-temporal buckets were filled with zeros, which improves model fit but is a modelling convenience rather than ground truth. Coordinates throughout are area centroids rather than exact GPS points, so no encoding recovers true spatial precision beyond the community area or census tract. Model-side, the SVR's quadratic scaling meant it never saw more than a 50,000-row sample, so part of its gap to the network reflects data availability rather than architecture alone. The NN's own depth search was run once on a baseline configuration rather than per experiment, due to compute constraints. On the RL side, the agent was trained on very specific environment settings for a fixed home-charging window with a fixed cost function and demand distribution, so it is not yet validated against fleet-scale coordination of many vehicles or real time-of-use electricity tariffs.


## Future Work
Three directions would most improve the pilot's next iteration. First, moving the SVR to a linearly scaling method, such as a gradient-boosted tree like XGBoost, would allow it to train on the full dataset and would also make the results more explainable. Further, it might be a fairer benchmark against the network, while an independent architecture search per neural network configuration would tighten that side of the comparison. Second, enriching the feature set with a genuine time trend and dynamic POI data, alongside external sources such as scheduled events (excluded here for incomplete timestamps) and public transit disruptions. Third, the smart charging agent should be extended from a single vehicle to a fleet-level setting with shared charging infrastructure, variable tariffs, and vehicle-specific battery and route profiles. This would be closer to a real-world scenario for a ride-hailing platform. It would then also influence the choice of learner. As the state and action spaces grow, Monte Carlo or other tabular agents would most likely lose in comparison.
